questions.question: An invented aircraft weighs 12,000 lb and flies at 400 ft/s with a thrust of 5,000 lb and a drag of 2,000 lb. What is its specific excess power Ps?
options: 100 ft/s
167 ft/s
67 ft/s
233 ft/s
questions.explanation: Ps = (T − D) V/W = 3,000 × 400/12,000 = 100 ft/s. Only the thrust in excess of the drag is left to climb or accelerate.

questions.question: At the same altitude, speed, and weight, how does a sustained turn boundary compare with the cruise boundary?
options: It lies above, and the gap grows with the wing loading
It lies above, and the gap shrinks with the wing loading
It lies above by the same amount at every wing loading
It coincides, because Ps = 0 in both cases
questions.explanation: The turn multiplies the induced term by n², and that term grows with the wing loading. A shift by the same amount at every wing loading is the climb or the acceleration case.

questions.question: The field requirements of an invented aircraft move from sea level to a higher density altitude, with the same distances. How do the takeoff and landing boundaries move?
options: The takeoff line steepens and the landing line moves left
The takeoff line flattens and the landing line moves right
The takeoff line steepens and the landing line stays in place
The takeoff line stays in place and the landing line moves left
questions.explanation: A lower density steepens the takeoff line, through ρ and through the lower thrust lapse α, and it lowers the wing loading that the braking roll allows. The landing line is independent of the thrust and still moves with the density.

questions.question: A design point is placed inside the feasible region, at a distance from the active boundaries. What does this margin cover?
options: The uncertainty in inputs such as CD0, CLmax, and the thrust lapse α
The gap between the threshold and the objective boundaries
The thrust lost between sea-level static and the condition
The fuel burned between takeoff and the condition
questions.explanation: Each boundary is computed from estimated inputs, and an error in one of them moves the boundary. The thrust lapse and the fuel burned are already in each boundary through α and β.

questions.question: With a fixed engine, the sizing loop returns a higher WTO than the pass before. What happens to the available TSL/WTO?
options: It falls, because TSL stays at the published value
It holds, because the engine is scaled with WTO
It rises, because a heavier aircraft needs more thrust
It holds, because the design point fixes the ratio
questions.explanation: A fixed engine has a published TSL, and the ratio falls as WTO grows. Thrust that scales with the weight describes a rubber engine.

questions.question: For the Cessna 162, the climb and the landing boundaries set the lowest feasible T/W, and the turn and the climb set the lowest feasible sea-level power. Why do the two diagrams differ?
options: Each boundary is converted with its own speed, efficiency, and density ratio
Every boundary is divided by the same altitude factor of the piston engine
The landing boundary moves to a lower wing loading when thrust becomes power
The turn boundary is computed at a higher load factor on the power diagram
questions.explanation: Power is thrust times true airspeed over propeller efficiency, corrected to sea level with the density ratio of the condition. Each boundary is multiplied by a different factor, and the order of the boundaries changes.

questions.question: In the T-45C example, the ceiling and the maximum speed boundaries are the first to check. Why?
options: They are the highest boundaries, and both rest on estimates
They are vertical boundaries, and the thrust cannot move them
They lie above the actual point, and the example fails there
They use power-on stall speeds, and the standard uses power off
questions.explanation: The two highest boundaries rest on an estimated thrust lapse α at altitude and an estimated CDc. An error in either estimate changes the margin of the T-45C before any other boundary does.

questions.question: The T-45C landing boundary is WTO/S ≤ 99 lb/ft² with kTD = 1.23. With kTD = 1.10 and the same braking roll, about where does the boundary lie?
options: 124 lb/ft²
111 lb/ft²
79 lb/ft²
89 lb/ft²
questions.explanation: The limit on WTO/S varies with 1/kTD². A lower kTD raises it by the factor (1.23/1.10)² = 1.25, to about 124 lb/ft².
